topic: Socratic answer-withholding pedagogy in human/AI tutoring + instilling strict behavioral constraints in small language models via fine-tuning

researchers.name: Manu Kapur
researchers.known_for: Productive Failure — structured problem-solving BEFORE instruction improves conceptual understanding and transfer, but only when followed by teacher-led consolidation; explicitly NOT unguided discovery. 2021 meta-analysis with Sinha; 2024 trade book.

researchers.name: Paul Kirschner
researchers.known_for: Lead author of Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work' — the canonical case that novices need explicit direct instruction; minimal-guidance methods cause cognitive overload.

researchers.name: John Sweller
researchers.known_for: Cognitive Load Theory and the worked-example effect — novices learn best from studying worked solutions, not unguided search; co-author of the 2006 minimal-guidance critique.

researchers.name: Richard E. Clark
researchers.known_for: Co-author of the 2006 minimal-guidance critique; long-standing skeptic of discovery, inquiry, and constructivist teaching methods.

researchers.name: Robert Bjork
researchers.known_for: Desirable difficulties — conditions that slow initial performance (retrieval practice, spacing, generation) but improve long-term retention; theoretical warrant for making learners struggle.

researchers.name: Michelene (Micki) Chi
researchers.known_for: ICAP framework (Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive) — generative/interactive engagement beats passive receipt; supports questioning over telling.

researchers.name: Kurt VanLehn
researchers.known_for: 2011 meta-analysis: human tutoring is d≈0.79 (not Bloom's 2 sigma) and step-based intelligent tutoring systems are nearly as effective (d≈0.76); deflated the human-tutor mystique.

researchers.name: Kenneth Koedinger
researchers.known_for: Cognitive Tutors and the 'assistance dilemma' (with Aleven, 2007): when does giving information help vs. withholding it — frames answer-withholding as an optimization problem, not a doctrine.

researchers.name: Dorottya Demszky
researchers.known_for: NLP for education; 'conversational uptake' measures of how tutors build on student talk; empirical grounding for what good tutor moves look like in dialogue data.

researchers.name: Rose E. Wang
researchers.known_for: Bridge and Tutor CoPilot — LLMs underperform expert human tutors on remediation decisions; expert-thought-annotated data can close part of the gap.
researchers.camp: Education NLP / skeptical of vanilla LLM tutoring

researchers.name: Arnav Gudibande & Eric Wallace
researchers.affiliation: UC Berkeley (with Snell, Geng, Liu, Abbeel, Levine, Song)
researchers.known_for: 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs' (2023): small models fine-tuned on teacher outputs copy style and fool crowdworkers but close little of the actual capability gap.

researchers.name: Chunting Zhou et al.
researchers.known_for: LIMA (2023) and the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis: knowledge lives in pretraining; fine-tuning mostly teaches format and style — 1,000 curated examples can suffice.
researchers.camp: Distillation optimists (style is cheap to instill)

researchers.name: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, Jeff Dean
researchers.known_for: 'Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network' (2015) — the founding paper of knowledge distillation via soft teacher targets.

researchers.name: LearnLM team
researchers.known_for: Pedagogy-informed fine-tuning of Gemini; evidence that tutoring behavior (including not blurting answers) can be trained into weights and preferred by expert raters over GPT-4o by ~31 points.

researchers.name: Mrinmaya Sachan group (Dinucu-Jianu, Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Gurevych)
researchers.affiliation: ETH Zurich / ETH AI Center / TU Darmstadt
researchers.known_for: 'From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving' (2025) — online RL turning a 7B model into a tutor that withholds solutions (10.6% leakage) while improving simulated student solve rates 25.3%, near-matching LearnLM; SFT-based SocraticLM baseline lost capability (-9.4% MATH500) where RL did not.

researchers.name: Andrew Lan
researchers.known_for: Training LLM tutors to optimize actual student learning outcomes in dialogues (AIED 2025), rather than surface helpfulness.

researchers.name: Hoda Fakour & Moslem Imani
researchers.affiliation: National Taiwan Normal University / National Taiwan University
researchers.known_for: 2025 mixed-methods study (N=230): human tutors rated higher for critical-thinking encouragement (4.5 vs 4.2) and personalized feedback (4.6 vs 3.8); AI far higher for comfort asking questions (4.9 vs 2.8).

frameworks.name: Productive Failure
frameworks.description: Sequence problem-solving BEFORE instruction: students generate (mostly failed) solution attempts, which activate prior knowledge and prepare them to learn from subsequent consolidation. Requires careful task design plus teacher-led consolidation — the failure phase alone is not enough; explicitly NOT unguided discovery.
frameworks.citation: Kapur (2008) Cognition and Instruction; Sinha & Kapur (2021) Review of Educational Research 91(5); Kapur (2012) Instructional Science

frameworks.name: Cognitive Load Theory / worked-example effect
frameworks.description: Working memory is severely limited for novel information; unguided problem search wastes capacity on means-ends analysis instead of schema building. Novices learn more from worked examples; guidance can fade as expertise grows (expertise reversal effect, Kalyuga).
frameworks.citation: Sweller (1988) Cognitive Science; Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Educational Psychologist 41(2)

frameworks.name: Desirable Difficulties
frameworks.description: Manipulations that impair short-term performance (retrieval practice, spacing, generation) enhance long-term retention and transfer — but only when the learner can eventually succeed; difficulties become undesirable when the learner lacks the background to overcome them.
frameworks.citation: Bjork (1994) in Metacognition: Knowing About Knowing; Bjork & Bjork (2011)

frameworks.name: ICAP framework
frameworks.description: Learning outcomes ordered Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive. Socratic dialogue sits in the Interactive/Constructive band — its advantage comes from forcing generation, not from answer secrecy per se.

frameworks.name: Assistance Dilemma
frameworks.description: Frames tutoring as balancing giving vs. withholding information: both over-assistance (shallow learning) and under-assistance (floundering, frustration) hurt. Optimal assistance depends on learner prior knowledge, task stage, and error type — a direct challenge to blanket 'never give the answer' rules.

frameworks.name: Scaffolding / contingent tutoring
frameworks.description: Effective tutors are contingent: they escalate help only after failure and fade it after success (Wood's 'contingent shift' rule). Socratic questioning is one rung on a help ladder, not the whole ladder.
frameworks.citation: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 17(2)

frameworks.name: Knowledge Distillation
frameworks.description: Train a small student on a large teacher's output distribution (soft targets) or generated data (sequence-level KD). Modern behavior distillation fine-tunes small open models on teacher-generated dialogues to transfer interaction patterns.
frameworks.citation: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015) arXiv:1503.02531; Kim & Rush (2016) sequence-level KD

frameworks.name: Superficial Alignment Hypothesis (LIMA)
frameworks.description: A model's knowledge and capabilities come almost entirely from pretraining; alignment fine-tuning teaches which subdistribution of formats/styles to use. Corollary: a small, highly curated SFT set can instill a stable interaction style — which explains both why small-data behavior tuning works for format and why it fails to add capability.
frameworks.citation: Zhou et al. (2023) 'LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment' arXiv:2305.11206

frameworks.name: Shallow safety/constraint alignment
frameworks.description: Fine-tuned behavioral constraints often live in the first few output tokens and collapse under prefill, paraphrase, or multi-turn pressure; making constraints 'more than a few tokens deep' requires training on trajectories where the model recovers mid-response.
frameworks.citation: Qi et al. (2024) 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' arXiv:2406.05946

frameworks.name: LoRA vs full fine-tuning trade-off
frameworks.description: LoRA learns less new behavior than full fine-tuning but also forgets less of the base model's capabilities — directly relevant to instilling a tutoring persona without catastrophic forgetting of subject knowledge in a small model.
frameworks.citation: Biderman et al. (2024) 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less' arXiv:2405.09673 (TMLR)

frameworks.name: Pedagogical RL alignment (student-simulation reward)
frameworks.description: Tutor LLM trained via online RL against a simulated student, rewarded jointly for student solve-rate gains and low solution leakage (a lambda tradeoff balances pedagogy vs helpfulness); preserves base capabilities better than SFT-based Socratic tuning.
frameworks.citation: Dinucu-Jianu et al. (2025) 'From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving' arXiv:2505.15607

frameworks.name: Behavior-aware sampling for constraint-preserving fine-tuning
frameworks.description: Selecting constraint examples by instruction-response behavior plus semantic diversity to prevent catastrophic forgetting; as little as 0.05% added targeted data recovered much of the lost constraint behavior (up to 41% harmfulness reduction).

frameworks.name: Pedagogical ability evaluation taxonomy for AI tutors
frameworks.description: Unified taxonomy (Maurya et al.) for judging LLM tutor responses on dimensions like mistake identification, providing guidance, and NOT revealing the answer too early — benchmarking tutor models beyond generic helpfulness.

debates.topic: Should learning start with instruction or with struggle?
debates.conventional: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006): novices should be explicitly shown what to do; minimal-guidance methods fail because they overload working memory and let errors compound.
debates.challenger: Kapur/Sinha: problem-solving-first (with subsequent instruction) beats instruction-first on conceptual understanding and transfer when tasks and consolidation are well designed (2021 meta-analysis, g≈0.36 overall).
debates.agreement_note: Both agents found this debate; both note the camps AGREE explicit instruction/structure is required — the real disagreement is sequencing, not whether to guide.

debates.topic: Is human tutoring really a 2-sigma intervention?
debates.conventional: Bloom (1984): one-on-one tutoring produces 2-standard-deviation gains — the benchmark every AI tutor cites.
debates.challenger: VanLehn (2011): human tutoring is actually d≈0.79, step-based ITS reach d≈0.76 — near parity. The 2-sigma figure bundled tutoring with mastery learning under unusual conditions.

debates.conventional: Socratic purism (embodied in Khanmigo's design): the tutor should question at nearly every turn and never reveal answers, forcing generation.
debates.challenger: Assistance-dilemma and contingent-scaffolding research: blanket withholding under-assists; effective tutors give bottom-out help after repeated failure. Recent LLM-tutor studies find Socratic guidance raises later learning gains but learners rate it less efficient and may defect to answer-giving tools.

debates.topic: Can small models be made into real tutors by imitating a big teacher?
debates.conventional: Fine-tune an open SLM on teacher-generated tutoring dialogues and you get a cheap Khanmigo (the Alpaca/Vicuna-era assumption).
debates.challenger: Gudibande et al. (2023): imitation transfers style and surface form, not capability — crowdworkers are fooled, targeted evals are not. Middle position (LIMA, LearnLM, ETH RL tutor): a tutoring PERSONA is mostly style, which is exactly what distillation transfers well — so a Socratic SLM is feasible precisely because the constraint is behavioral, while its subject-matter ceiling stays that of the base model.
debates.challenger_name: Gudibande & Wallace vs. Zhou et al. (LIMA) / LearnLM / ETH RL tutor

debates.topic: Do behavioral constraints trained into weights actually hold?
debates.conventional: SFT on consistent demonstrations makes the behavior reliable.
debates.challenger: Constraint adherence is often shallow — concentrated in early tokens and brittle under multi-turn pressure, user insistence, or distribution shift; small models are worse at maintaining persona under adversarial prodding, so training data must include pressure-and-recovery examples, not just clean demonstrations.
debates.confidence: single-source (gemini), corroborated by claude's catastrophic-forgetting findings

debates.topic: Is rated 'helpfulness' a valid signal of tutoring quality?
debates.conventional: Preference-trained LLMs and their judges reward helpful, complete answers; satisfaction ratings measure tutor quality.
debates.challenger: Pedagogy researchers: helpfulness-as-judged anticorrelates with sound tutoring (withholding answers, prompting reasoning). A pre-registered audit found LLM-judged helpfulness an unreliable pedagogy signal; crowdworker preference similarly overrated imitation models.
debates.challenger_name: Maurya et al. taxonomy line; Gudibande et al.
debates.confidence: single-source (claude), corroborated by gemini misconception on preference ratings

debates.conventional: AI tutors will replace human tutors as capability grows.
debates.challenger: Fakour & Imani (2025): humans still superior for critical-thinking encouragement, personalized feedback, emotional intelligence, trust; AI superior for self-paced learning and judgment-free question-asking (4.9 vs 2.8) — complementary roles rather than replacement.

findings.claim: Problem-solving before instruction (productive failure) outperforms instruction-then-practice on conceptual knowledge and transfer across 53+ studies; effects strengthen with higher grade levels and design fidelity.
findings.source: Sinha & Kapur (2021), Review of Educational Research 91(5); Kapur (2012) Instructional Science
findings.effect_size: overall g ≈ 0.36 favoring PF; ≈0.8+ in high-fidelity implementations

findings.claim: Human tutoring effect is d≈0.79 (not 2.0); step-based intelligent tutoring systems achieve d≈0.76 — software tutors that scaffold at the step level nearly match humans.
Median effect of intelligent tutoring systems across 50 evaluations: +0.66 SD.
findings.source: Kulik & Fletcher (2016), Review of Educational Research

findings.claim: Imitation models (1.5B-13B) fine-tuned on ChatGPT outputs mimic style well enough to fool crowdworkers but close little to none of the base-to-teacher capability gap on targeted evals; they mimic style but not factuality.
findings.source: Gudibande et al. (2023), 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs', arXiv:2305.15717
findings.effect_size: crowdworker preference ≈ parity with ChatGPT; ≈0% gap closure on weakly-covered tasks

findings.claim: 1,000 carefully curated SFT examples suffice to align a 65B model to a consistent assistant style — interaction format is learned cheaply while knowledge comes from pretraining.
findings.effect_size: LIMA equivalent or preferred vs GPT-4 in 43% of human comparisons

findings.claim: Pedagogy-informed fine-tuning measurably shifts tutor behavior at scale: expert raters preferred LearnLM over GPT-4o by ~31 percentage points — 'do not just give the answer' can be trained into weights.

A 7B model RL-aligned for pedagogy reached 25.3% simulated-student solve-rate improvement with only 10.6% solution leakage, near-matching LearnLM, while base benchmarks moved only -0.6% to +1.4%; the SFT baseline SocraticLM lost -2.1% MMLU and -9.4% MATH500.
findings.effect_size: 10.6% leakage; +25.3% solve rate; SFT baseline -9.4% MATH500

findings.claim: Students tutored by a Socratic-constrained LLM achieved higher learning gains in later sessions and adopted more understanding-driven strategies than with an unconstrained LLM — but perceived the Socratic tutor as less efficient.
Off-the-shelf LLMs substantially underperform expert human tutors on dialogic moves — deciding when to probe vs. tell, and remediating the actual student error rather than a generic one.
findings.source: Wang et al., 'Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap' (NAACL 2024)

findings.claim: Fine-tuning on benign, on-task data catastrophically erodes prior safety/refusal behavior; instruction-adherence changes are the main driver. Forgetting generally worsens with model scale within 1B-7B.
Mixing a tiny, behaviorally targeted set of constraint examples (0.05% additional data) into fine-tuning cuts harmfulness up to 41% — targeted data selection preserves constraints cheaply.
LoRA fine-tuning forgets less of base-model capabilities than full fine-tuning at the cost of learning less target-domain behavior — a favorable trade for style-only behavior transfer.
findings.source: Biderman et al. (2024), 'LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less', arXiv:2405.09673
findings.effect_size: consistent learning-vs-forgetting Pareto gap across domains

findings.claim: Behavioral constraints instilled by fine-tuning concentrate in the first few output tokens and collapse under prefill or persistent multi-turn attack; deepening alignment across the whole response distribution hardens constraints.

Students rated human tutors higher for critical-thinking encouragement (4.5 vs 4.2), personalized feedback (4.6 vs 3.8), complex-concept understanding (4.8 vs 4.0); ChatGPT won on self-paced learning (4.8 vs 3.9) and comfort asking questions (4.9 vs 2.8).
findings.source: Fakour & Imani (2025), Frontiers in Education, N=230

adjacent_domains.insight: Decades of evidence that asking evocative questions outperforms telling for behavior change — but MI codifies WHEN to shift from asking to informing (elicit-provide-elicit), a ready-made template for a tutor's escalation policy instead of blanket answer-withholding.

Clinical teaching scripts force the learner to commit to a diagnosis BEFORE the preceptor teaches — commit-then-instruct mirrors productive failure and shows structured question protocols can be trained into time-pressed non-expert tutors, analogous to fine-tuning a small model on a fixed dialogue protocol.

Explaining a problem aloud to a non-answering listener resolves many bugs — the generation/self-explanation effect does the work, not the listener's intelligence; a small model that reliably prompts self-explanation can deliver value beyond its raw capability.

Jailbreak and persona-drift research is the closest empirical literature on 'will my model hold its constraint under user pressure' — red-teaming with escalating please-just-tell-me pressure and training on recovery trajectories transfers directly to testing an answer-withholding tutor.

Well-designed games teach mechanics through structured challenge without tutorials: difficulty is sequenced so failure is informative and quick to retry — a design vocabulary for making a withheld answer feel like a solvable puzzle rather than stonewalling.

misconceptions.belief: The Socratic method means never revealing the answer.
misconceptions.reality: Expert tutors are contingent: they withhold while progress is possible and give bottom-out hints after repeated failure (assistance dilemma, contingent scaffolding). Historical Socratic dialogues themselves mix questions with substantial telling. Withholding helps only within a structured sequence with adequate guidance.

misconceptions.belief: One-on-one tutoring gives 2-sigma gains, so an AI tutor should target d = 2.0.
misconceptions.reality: VanLehn (2011): the replicated human-tutoring effect is d≈0.79; Bloom's 2 sigma bundled tutoring with mastery learning. Realistic AI-tutor targets are ~0.7-0.8.
misconceptions.confidence: single-source (gemini), corroborated by claude's VanLehn finding

misconceptions.belief: Struggle is always good for learning (misreading of desirable difficulties / productive failure).
misconceptions.reality: Difficulties are desirable only when the learner has prerequisites to eventually succeed and the struggle is followed by consolidation; unguided floundering without follow-up instruction is unproductive failure.

misconceptions.belief: Fine-tuning a small model on big-teacher tutoring transcripts makes it tutor as well as the teacher.
misconceptions.reality: Imitation transfers surface style and dialogue moves, not subject-matter capability or error diagnosis (Gudibande et al. 2023). The Socratic persona is learnable; the model's math is still the base model's math — scope the domain to what the base model already knows.

misconceptions.belief: A strong system prompt is enough to enforce answer-withholding; fine-tuning is overkill.
misconceptions.reality: Models drift from prompted personas under multi-turn pressure; weights-level tuning holds constraints far better, but even fine-tuned constraints are shallow unless training data includes user-pressure and recovery examples (Qi et al. 2024).

misconceptions.belief: More fine-tuning data always yields better constraint adherence.
misconceptions.reality: Narrow, repetitive SFT causes catastrophic forgetting and mode collapse into templated responses; LIMA-style small curated sets and LoRA-style low-intrusion tuning often preserve more of the knowledge the tutor needs.
misconceptions.confidence: single-source (gemini), corroborated by claude's forgetting findings

misconceptions.belief: If students prefer the tutor and rate it helpful, it is teaching well.
misconceptions.reality: Learner preference and learning gains dissociate: answer-giving tutors are rated more efficient while producing shallower gains; crowdworker preference overrates imitation models; LLM-judged helpfulness is an unreliable pedagogy signal. Evaluate with delayed post-tests and targeted probes.

misconceptions.belief: Fine-tuning on benign, on-task data leaves prior constraints intact.
misconceptions.reality: Catastrophic forgetting degrades constraint adherence even from benign fine-tuning; retention requires deliberate mitigation such as behavior-aware mixing of constraint exemplars (0.05% extra data can recover much of it).

misconceptions.belief: Direct instruction and productive struggle are irreconcilable opposites.
misconceptions.reality: Productive failure embeds explicit instruction after structured struggle; Kirschner/Sweller/Clark allow guidance fading with expertise. The empirical disagreement is about sequencing and learner prior knowledge, not whether guidance is needed.

conflicts: Gudibande et al. (imitation transfers no capability) vs LIMA/LearnLM (small curated tuning works) — both agents resolved this as a style-vs-capability split rather than a contradiction: behavioral constraints ARE style, capability is not transferable.

ETH RL-tutor paper reports SFT-based Socratic tuning (SocraticLM) degrades base capability (-9.4% MATH500) while RL preserves it — tension with the LIMA claim that small SFT is benign; likely depends on data narrowness and scale.
gaps: No literature found on STRICT syntactic constraints (every sentence must be a question) — the project's spec is stricter than anything in the pedagogy literature, which studies answer-withholding, not questions-only form.

Little empirical work on Socratic constraints under emotional-support conversations (the project's weakest category) — the pedagogy literature treats affect via human tutors, the ML literature via safety refusals.
No learning-outcome data for the app itself — all project metrics are constraint-adherence metrics, not student learning gains.

Answer-smuggling (leaking the answer INSIDE a question) appears in the project's data as the dominant failure but has no named equivalent in the literature; nearest neighbors are 'solution leakage' (ETH RL tutor) and shallow-alignment token-depth arguments.
